content:
Covered in wet toilet paper from the mirrors to the walls and ceiling
Witness who saw the scene cleaned up the mess
Could face penalties under the Minor Offenses Act

Outrage is growing after reports emerged of female students suspected of playing a prank by throwing wet toilet paper onto the mirrors, walls, and ceiling of a public restroom at a children's playground. A citizen who witnessed the scene cleaned it up, while critics say the act should not be dismissed as a mere prank because it disrupts the proper use of public facilities.

Photos showing a public restroom mirror, walls, ceiling, and other surfaces covered in wet toilet paper have sparked outrage. The Threads account "lebabagency" posted the images.

View original image

On November 25, posts and photos about an incident at a public restroom in a children's playground appeared on social networking services and social media. The author, identified only as A, said they heard repeated laughter and sounds like something being struck in the restroom, and went to check because they worried an assault might be taking place. According to A, two female students sensed someone approaching and left the restroom.

Photos posted by A showed clumps of wet toilet paper stuck not only to the mirror but also to the wall tiles, ceiling, sink, and areas around the faucets. A reportedly regretted not checking the restroom sooner and mentioned the difficulties faced by cleaning workers. Concerned that the wet paper would become even harder to remove once it dried and stuck to the fixtures, A also cleaned up the mess.

After the incident became known, internet users responded with criticism, much of it focused on the students' lack of public etiquette. Some shared their own experiences, saying they had seen students engage in similar behavior at schools and private academies. Others said that toilet paper was no longer provided in school restrooms because of such behavior.

Deliberately contaminating a public restroom can lead to legal liability, going beyond a mere violation of public etiquette. Another internet user pointed out the seriousness of the problem, saying that wet toilet paper is sometimes thrown at people rather than fixtures. Some also said adults need to actively stop and discipline children who behave improperly. The students may see it as a momentary prank, but the consequences fall squarely on the many members of the public who use the facilities and on cleaning workers. In particular, once wet toilet paper dries and sticks to fixtures, extra labor is needed to remove it. If large quantities enter the drains, they can also cause problems such as blockages.

Above all, deliberately contaminating a public restroom can lead to legal liability, going beyond a mere violation of public etiquette. Article 3(1)(11) of the current Minor Offenses Act makes it punishable to carelessly discard items such as toilet paper, cigarette butts, chewing gum, and other trash anywhere. Article 3(1)(9) of the same Act also prohibits carelessly dirtying or damaging structures built by other people or organizations.

Such acts may be punishable by a fine of up to 100,000 won, detention, or a minor fine. The Act on Public Toilets, Etc. also prohibits damaging or defacing facilities and engaging in conduct that obstructs the hygienic use of toilets as prescribed by local government ordinances. If a prank is serious enough to impair the normal functioning of a facility, it may also be subject to charges of property damage under the Criminal Act.


Under Article 366 of the Criminal Act, anyone who damages another person's property or otherwise impairs its utility may be sentenced to up to three years in prison or fined up to 7 million won. Property damage does not require that a facility be physically broken. Depending on the specific circumstances, an act that temporarily prevents an item from being used for its intended purpose may also constitute property damage. However, anyone under the age of 14 is not subject to criminal punishment under the Criminal Act. Those aged 10 to under 14 who commit acts in violation of criminal laws may be subject to protective measures under the Juvenile Act.
